title: The householder's path
hook: the Gurus chose family life over renunciation

segments.voice: Yesterday, seva as spirituality: the shoe counter, Bhai Ghanaiya's water skin. Your line was service is the path. Did you manage one unthanked thing without mentioning it? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.

We're back in the circle of yogis from a few days ago, the Siddhas of the Siddh Gosht. These were men who had walked away from everything: wives, children, fields, money, houses. They lived apart, and to them that was the whole point. A person tied to a family, they held, was tied down. And here is Guru Nanak in front of them, a man tradition remembers with a wife and sons, who would go home and farm. In the janamsakhis, the old stories of his life, the yogis invite him to join them, to take up their dress and their road. The door to the renouncer's life is wide open. Today is about which way he turns.
screen: `THE YOGIS LEFT EVERYTHING.` → `A GURU WITH A FAMILY.` → `THE DOOR IS OPEN.`

segments.voice: First, the word. Grihasth means the householder's life: marriage, children, work, a kitchen, bills, neighbors. To the yogis, the high road to God meant leaving all that behind. Second, the lotus. In the Siddh Gosht itself, Guru Nanak answers with a picture. In paraphrase: as the lotus flower stays untouched in the water, and the duck swims on the stream without its feathers getting soaked, so a person can live in the world with attention on the Word. The lotus doesn't leave the pond. It just isn't drowned by it. Third, the soot. In Raag Suhi, Guru Nanak says it another way. In paraphrase: in the midst of the soot, stay spotless. The soot is everyday life, the smoke of the kitchen and the market. The teaching isn't to run from the smoke. It's to stay clean inside it. Fourth, the life he chose. Tradition says Guru Nanak, after his travels, settled at Kartarpur, worked the fields, and lived among family and sangat. Tradition remembers the Gurus after him living in the world too, not in caves. So Sikh teaching sets no monk's life above the householder's: holiness is meant to happen at a kitchen table, in a marriage, while raising children. That isn't the easy road. A cave has no toddlers. And this week walked the same road: the mind made a friend, attention, the Word as Guru, book and people, two swords, the shoe counter, and now the home. Holiness at home.
screen: `GRIHASTH: THE HOUSEHOLDER'S LIFE.` · `THE LOTUS STAYS IN THE POND.` · `SPOTLESS IN THE SOOT.` · `KARTARPUR: FIELDS AND FAMILY.` · then, large: `HOLINESS AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for your household. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people you share a home with, or the people you'd call home if you live alone: a parent, a partner, a child, a roommate, a friend who checks on you. See each face. Ask, for each one, what small thing would make their day lighter. A meal. A call. Taking a chore off their list. Choose one. Hold it as you breathe, the way a lotus holds still on moving water. If you pray, you can hold them with Waheguru. After the bell, go and do the one thing. The bell holds the time.
Grihasth. The householder's life of family, work and home, which the Gurus lived as a path to the One. Today's word.
Your line: holiness at home. Today, treat one ordinary moment at home, a meal, a bedtime, a dish, as part of the path, not a break from it. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Sikh teaching honors the householder's path, marrying, working and raising a family in the world, in the pattern tradition remembers from Guru Nanak's life at Kartarpur.

notes: Editor: 'there's no monk class' (and the matching myth item) recast as 'Sikh teaching sets no monk's life above the householder's', since ascetic orders such as the Udasis exist in Sikh history; Guru Nanak's wife and sons framed as tradition in the hook; 'harder, not easier' softened.

Paraphrase of 'anjan maahi niranjan rahiai' (Suhi, Guru Nanak, Ang 730); please confirm the Ang.
The yogis inviting Guru Nanak to join them is presented as janamsakhi tradition; please confirm. The hook says Guru Nanak had a wife and sons, which is from tradition, not the Granth.
The line that tradition remembers the Gurus after Guru Nanak living in the world is a general statement; please confirm the framing, given Guru Har Krishan's short life.
The yogis' view that the high road to God meant leaving home behind is a general framing of Siddha practice; please confirm.
